body.objective: Students will be able to analyze form and function in designed objects.
body.iCan: I can analyze form and function in designed objects.
successCriteria: I can explain form and function in designed objects
I can critique a design and suggest improvements
body.hook: Look around the room. Your chair, water bottle, phone case and backpack were all designed by someone who made choices about shape, material and colour. Good design is everywhere, and most of the time we don't even notice it, until something is badly designed.

vocabulary.definition: Planning how something will look and work.
The shape and physical appearance of an object.

study.title: Form Meets Function
study.question: How do designers balance how something looks with how it works?
study.passage:
Part 1, Object study (15 minutes): Each group gets three everyday objects (for example, a stapler, a reusable water bottle and a pair of scissors). For each object, answer:
• Function: What job does it do? Who is the user?
• Form: What shape, materials and colours were chosen?
• Ergonomics: How does it fit the hand or body?
• Aesthetic: Is it pleasing to look at? Why?
• Improvement: What would you change?
Part 2, Good vs bad design (10 minutes): Find one example of a frustrating design in the school (a door that you push when you should pull, a confusing sign, an uncomfortable chair). Explain why its form doesn't match its function.
Part 3, Sketch a redesign (20 minutes): Choose one object and draw three thumbnail sketches of an improved version. Label the changes and explain how each improves function or aesthetics.
Designers often say "form follows function": the shape should come from the job the object needs to do.

examples.title: Form and function
examples.problem: What is the function and form of a coffee mug?
examples.answer: Function: holds hot liquid; form: cylinder with a handle so hands don't burn
examples.explore: How does the handle show ergonomics?

examples.title: Bad design
examples.problem: A door with a pull handle that must be pushed. What's wrong?
steps: The form suggests the wrong action
examples.answer: The handle's form tells users to pull, which doesn't match its function

examples.title: Ergonomics
examples.problem: How are scissors designed for the hand?
examples.answer: Loops shaped for thumb and fingers make cutting comfortable
examples.explore: How could they be designed for left-handed users?

examples.title: Aesthetic choice
examples.problem: Why might a water bottle come in many colours?
examples.answer: Colour choices make it appealing and personal without changing function
